teaser: A swing, a spring, and a speaker share a smooth rhythm.
title: Why Electronics Use Sine Waves
question: Where else do you see a smooth back-and-forth wiggle?
idea: A sine wave records a smooth, repeating wiggle. Spinning generators and speakers making pure tones use this rhythm.

curiosity.intro: Follow one smooth wiggle from the living room into sound and power.
curiosity.carryForward: Keep a small drawing of a rhythm you noticed.

questions.question: What is a sine wave?
questions.notice: Notice how the swing slows near the end of its trip.
questions.say: A sine wave is a smooth back-and-forth wiggle that repeats. It can show how a position or an electric push changes over time. A gentle swing moves in a sine-like rhythm; its seat travels along an arc.
questions.try: With Big nearby, take a gentle swing, bounce a soft toy spring over a tray, or move a rope from side to side on the floor. Draw the smooth wiggle you notice. Keep wall power and plugged-in devices closed and untouched; these are activities with a swing, spring, rope, paper, or an intact battery speaker.

questions.question: How can spinning make a wave?
questions.notice: Find the turning disk beside the wire coil.
questions.say: A generator turns motion into electrical energy. As a magnet spins beside wire, the electric push changes smoothly, first one way and then the other. Many generators make the AC power supplied at home. AC means that the push changes direction repeatedly.
questions.try: Draw a dot on a paper circle. Turn the circle slowly and watch the dot rise and fall.

questions.question: What wiggles inside a speaker?
questions.notice: Look at the circle on the front of the speaker.
questions.say: The speaker cone moves in and out, making the air nearby squeeze and spread. Those changes travel to your ears as sound. For a pure, steady tone, the cone moves in a sine-like rhythm. Music and voices make more complicated wiggles.
questions.try: Let Big set an intact battery speaker to low volume. Rest fingertips lightly on its outer case, leaving the cone alone, and notice any quiet buzz. A drawing of the cone’s motion works too.

questions.question: Why use a smooth wiggle?
questions.notice: Follow the rounded turns in Little’s notebook.
questions.say: Spinning parts can make sine waves naturally. Smooth changes help many motors and speakers work evenly. Sudden jumps can make extra buzz or jerky starts. Electronics also use steady power and other signal shapes; not every signal is a sine wave.
questions.try: Draw a smooth wave and a zigzag. Trace them slowly with a finger and compare the turns.

beats.title: A line with a rhythm
beats.passage: Little Wonderer drew a line that rose, curved over, and dipped down. Again and again, it made the same smooth wiggle. “That shape is called a sine wave,” said Big Wonderer. Sine is the math name for this smooth shape. Could a line on paper help explain a swing, a speaker, and electricity?

foldable.heading: A smooth wiggle
foldable.body: Little drew a smooth line that rose and fell again. Big called it a sine wave. Could this shape help explain a speaker?

beats.title: Slow at the turn
beats.passage: Outside, Little took a gentle swing. Near each end, the swing slowed, paused, and came back. It moved fastest through the middle. Its seat followed an arc. A sine-like line could show its back-and-forth position as time passed. The line was a record of the motion, not the shape of the seat’s path.
beats.prompt: How is a record of motion different from the seat’s path?

foldable.heading: Slow at the turn
foldable.body: The swing slowed at each end and sped through the middle. A sine-like line could record its back-and-forth motion as time passed.

beats.title: A bounce comes back
beats.passage: At the table, Big held a spring above a tray. A spring is a coil that can stretch and return. Its lower end bounced up and down, slowing near each turn. Little watched the bounces grow smaller. A steady sine wave repeats evenly; this real spring gradually settled as it lost energy to its surroundings.
beats.prompt: What changed about the spring’s bounces over time?

foldable.heading: A bouncing spring
foldable.body: Big held a spring above a tray. Its end bounced up and down. Each bounce grew smaller until the spring settled.

beats.title: A wiggle travels
beats.passage: Little moved one end of a rope gently from side to side along the floor. A wiggle traveled toward Big. Bits of rope moved back and forth while the wave moved along. Little drew its rounded shape. Smooth turning felt different from suddenly changing direction. The same kind of curve kept appearing in new places.
beats.prompt: What traveled along the rope, and what moved back and forth?

foldable.heading: Along the rope
foldable.body: Little moved a rope from side to side. A wiggle traveled toward Big, while each bit of rope moved back and forth.

beats.title: A turn makes a push
beats.passage: Big showed a generator: a machine that turns motion into electrical energy. Its magnet spins beside wire. The electric push grows, fades, and reverses smoothly. A sine wave records this change. Many spinning generators make AC power for homes. AC means the push changes direction again and again.
beats.prompt: How does spinning change the electric push?

foldable.heading: Turning into power
foldable.body: A generator turns motion into electrical energy. As a magnet spins beside wire, the electric push grows, fades, and changes direction smoothly.

beats.title: A quiet tone
beats.passage: The speaker made a quiet tone. Its cone moved in and out, nudging air. A pure tone follows a sine-like rhythm. Smooth changes help machines work evenly. Electronics use other shapes too. Little wondered, “Where else can we find this smooth wiggle?”
beats.prompt: Where else could you notice a smooth wiggle?

foldable.heading: A speaker’s rhythm
foldable.body: The speaker’s cone moved in and out to make a steady tone. Little drew its smooth rhythm. Where else might a wiggle appear?

math.title: Count groups of wiggles
math.intro: Add the same number for each equal group or row.

tasks.prompt: Little draws 2 groups of swing marks, with 3 marks in each group. How many marks are there?
tasks.hint: Add 3 + 3, one group at a time.
tasks.label: TASK 1

tasks.prompt: Big draws spring bounces in 4 rows, with 2 bounces in each row. How many bounces are drawn?
tasks.hint: Add 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 to count the four rows.
tasks.label: TASK 2

tasks.prompt: Little counts 3 sets of rope wiggles, with 3 wiggles in each set. How many wiggles is that?
tasks.hint: Use 3 + 3 + 3 to count all three sets.
tasks.label: TASK 3

tasks.prompt: A page has 3 rows of wave drawings, with 4 drawings in each row. How many drawings are on the page?
tasks.hint: Add 4 + 4 + 4 for the three equal rows.
tasks.label: TASK 4

tasks.prompt: Big counts 5 groups of crank turns, with 3 turns in each group. How many turns does Big count?
tasks.hint: Try 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3, adding one group at a time.
tasks.label: TASK 5

tasks.prompt: Little draws speaker wiggles in 4 rows, with 5 wiggles in each row. How many wiggles are drawn?
tasks.hint: Use 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 to count the four rows.
tasks.label: TASK 6

math.extension: Choose one task and draw its equal groups or rows.
math.printNote: Show your thinking with numbers, marks, or words.
math.parentNote: Age 8 / Grade 2 math. Six equal-group and array tasks use rows and columns from 2 to 5. Repeated addition gives totals from 6 to 20. These are story counts, not measurements of sound or power.
math.answerKeyIntro: Age 8 / Grade 2 math. Add once for each equal group or row. Welcome a drawing or spoken explanation.

answers.label: Reading · 2

parentGuidance: Age 8, Grade 3 reading, Grade 2 math. A grown-up stays nearby and sets speaker volume low. Keep wall power and plugged-in devices closed and untouched; these are activities with a swing, spring, rope, paper, or an intact battery speaker. Do not open an outlet or take apart a powered device. A small-angle swing is approximately sinusoidal over time; its physical path is an arc. Real spring motion loses energy and settles. AC voltage from an ideal uniformly spinning generator is sinusoidal: relative rotation of a magnet and coil changes magnetic flux through the wire. This is the changing electric push in the story. Grid power also comes from sources with electronic converters, and many devices convert AC to steady DC internally. A speaker cone’s motion for a pure tone is approximately sinusoidal; sound travels as pressure changes, not as a rope-shaped path through air. Smooth sine waves can reduce unwanted harmonics in machines and pure tones; digital electronics intentionally use other waveforms. The tracing diorama compares an ideal sine shape with a triangle wave. Its marker and moving paper show position over time, not an electrical experiment or measured device output.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits a sine wave?
questions.answer: A sine wave is a smooth, repeating wiggle.

questions.prompt: What does a generator change into electrical energy?
questions.answer: A generator changes turning motion into electrical energy; its electric push can change smoothly as it spins.

questions.prompt: How does a speaker make sound?
choices: Its cone moves in and out, nudging air
questions.answer: The cone moves in and out, nudging air. For a pure tone, it follows a sine-like rhythm.

questions.prompt: Do electronics use only sine waves?
choices: Yes, every signal has the same shape
No, they also use other shapes and steady power
questions.answer: Electronics also use other signal shapes and steady power. Sine waves are useful, but they are not the only kind.
